claims.text: Overall tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is governed by cyclic mechanical removal and electrochemical reformation of a protective oxide film.
The initially polished high-entropy alloy has a native passivating oxide film that provides corrosion resistance under static conditions.
Mechanical sliding under load disrupts the passive film in a chloride-containing electrolyte.
A no-sliding test in the same electrolyte isolates the pure-corrosion contribution.
The integrity of the protective passive oxide film is the structural mediator of the coupled response.
Removal of the passive film locally exposes the underlying metal to the electrolyte.
Exposure caused by film removal accelerates localized corrosion until a new protective film forms.
The balance between the mechanical film-removal rate and electrochemical repassivation rate dictates overall degradation.
An alloy with a more robust or faster-forming passive film should exhibit lower coupled degradation.
Combined tribo-corrosion will produce greater total material degradation than static corrosion without sliding.
The wear and corrosion components will both increase during combined exposure because repeated film removal exposes fresh metal.
Enhancing passive-film resilience will reduce total degradation, mass loss, and corrosion-product formation.
Under static corrosion conditions, the protective film remains nearly intact.
The prediction should hold for alloys whose corrosion protection depends on a stable passivating oxide film.
The prediction may fail in alloy systems that do not passivate.
The prediction may fail when mechanical wear dominates sufficiently that repassivation kinetics are irrelevant.
Increasing Cr or Al content can improve oxide-film stability.
Failure of a demonstrably enhanced passive film to reduce tribo-corrosion degradation would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
Finding no difference between static and tribo-corrosion conditions would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
